newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asia Grains - CBOT wheat surges in Asian trade.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grains - CBOT wheat surges in Asian trade.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures surged on Monday in Asian trade on reports that unseasonally cold spring weather in the U.S. and dry conditions in Australia and Europe may squeeze world wheat supplies.

The CBOT May contract rose the 20 U.S. cent daily limit to reach US$4.23 a bushel at 0700 GMT on the exchange's Project A after hours trading system. May closed the open outcry session 10 cents up on Friday in Chicago at $4.03 a bushel.

"Wheat futures were bullish early in the CBOT's Project A session on worries about the weather in the U.S., Australia and Europe," a trader with South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said.

The red winter wheat crop in the U.S. may be hit hard by a severe freeze which could kill the seed-producing head of the plant, while in Europe warnings by France to grain farmers to reduce irrigation amid early signs of drought were focusing the attention of the EU grain trade.

In Australia, Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) wheat futures moved up sharply on Monday on concerns over what could be emerging drought conditions in the east of the country and on the weather reports from the U.S. and Europe.

The possibility of trade sanctions against Iran dampening world wheat prices if Australia was forced to unload millions of tonnes of discount wheat was not enough to hold back a market which has been supported by major grain sales to India recently.
Corn buyers in Japan and South Korea will probably stay on the sidelines this week in the face of volatile international prices and as they currently have ample coverage, traders said.
"For corn, we are not expecting any buying interest from our clients for the time being," a trader in Seoul said.
"Corn business will be slow this week. We want to wait and see how the volatile soybean market will spill over," a trading house dealer in Tokyo added.
Japanese corn premiums were quoted in Japan at about 92 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract against 94 U.S. cents a week ago.

South Korea's Daehan Flour Mills Co Ltd and Korea Flour Milling Corp were both seen seeking a total of 40,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat this week, but any buying may be delayed due to the strong gains in wheat futures.
CBOT corn contracts also firmed in Asian dealings in line with the rise in wheat futures, dealers said.
May corn futures hit a peak of $3.07-3/4 a bushel, up from Friday's open outcry close of $2.99-1/2, while July hit a high of $3.10 before falling back to to $3.06-3/4.
Expectations that trans-Pacific freight rates may ease further are also keeping Japanese buyers out of the market.
U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rates are now quoted at about $24.00 a tonne. "We are waiting for the freight rates to slip to around $22.00 (a tonne) in the future," a trader said.

In South Korea, an official with the Pan Ocean Shipping Co Ltd said freight rates from the Pacific Northwest fell to $14.50-$15.00 a tonne from $15.50 last week largely because of thin demand for Panamax-sized cargoes.
Rates from the U.S. Gulf to South Korea were also seen falling to $24.50-$25.00 a tonne from $25.50 last week.
Demand for Handy-sized vessels is rising due to growing demand for Chinese corn, the Pan Ocean official said.
The Chinese have exported about 1.0-1.2 million tonnes of corn this year to South Korea.
In Taiwan, buyers are seen tendering for up to 68,000 tonnes of wheat in the next two weeks, traders said.
Philippine wheat importers, who are currently in the market for 65,000 tonnes of wheat for May/June shipment, said they may shift to other suppliers such as Australia if U.S. prices continue to rise.
"Because of rising U.S. wheat prices and tight domestic supplies we might be forced to increase local flour prices," an executive at a Manila mill said.
